title: Topic 3 Questions
intro:
Use this page to practise **concept clarity** and **economic reasoning** before your tutorial.

**How to use:** write your own answer first, then (optionally) get AI feedback, then reveal the indicative answer to compare. Indicative answers illustrate *one* acceptable line of reasoning — they are **not** model answers. Your tutorial discussion and your own reasoning remain primary.
readings:
- Lecture notes: Topic 3 — Keynes's Theory of Money
- Course textbook chapter on liquidity preference and the liquidity trap

questions.title: Classical vs. Keynesian Views
questions.prompt: Compare and contrast Classical and Keynesian views on the macroeconomic role of money.
questions.suggested_answer:
**Similarities:**

1. Both relate the transaction demand for money positively to nominal GDP.
2. Both can be framed using the Cambridge Equation of Exchange, though their treatment of velocity differs.

**Differences:**

1. **Store of value role:** Keynes emphasised money's store-of-value role, neglected by the Quantity Theory of Money. This leads to Liquidity Preference theory (money demand falls with the interest rate) and underlies the precautionary and speculative motives.
2. **Interest rate determination:** Classical theory determines the interest rate in the market for loanable funds; Keynesian theory determines it in the money market. IS-LM analysis reconciles the two.
3. **Full employment and neutrality:** The Classical dichotomy and neutrality of money rest on wage and price flexibility in all markets. Keynes disagreed: (i) a liquidity trap can let an excess demand for money coexist with excess supply in the goods market indefinitely despite falling prices; (ii) even outside the trap, prices adjust at different rates across markets, so relative prices shift and dichotomy/neutrality fail.

questions.title: Exceptional Features of the Money Market
questions.prompt: What features of the market for money make it exceptional in terms of how it reacts if there is a shock to the demand for money? Is this a problem for macroeconomic equilibrium? Why or why not?
questions.suggested_answer:
**Three exceptional features:**

**(a)** The price of money is literally one — a direct consequence of its role as unit of account. Unlike other markets, disequilibrium cannot be resolved by a change in money's own nominal price.

**(b)** The supply of money is unresponsive: it is exogenously supplied by a sovereign authority (a Central Bank today).

**(c)** There are no close substitutes for the liquidity services money provides (less true today than in Keynes' time).

**Is this a problem?** Not always. Because money is central to both asset and goods markets, an exogenous rise in money demand can trigger collective adjustments that restore equilibrium: an **increase in the interest rate** (shifting agents back from money to interest-bearing assets) and/or a **fall in the price level** (raising goods demand and so reducing money demand via Walras' Law).

**When it becomes a problem:** these mechanisms fail in a **liquidity trap**, where agents will hold unlimited money for its perceived security — so the interest rate cannot rise and falling prices cannot revive goods demand.

questions.title: The Liquidity Trap
questions.prompt: Explain in words alone (without using diagrams) how the normal adjustment mechanisms that allow equilibrium to be restored following an increase in the demand for money do not work if the economy is in a liquidity trap.
questions.suggested_answer:
The **liquidity trap** combines low output with low interest rates. Keynes argued agents may become unwilling to part with money (beyond essentials) for either goods or other assets — **absolute liquidity preference**. Individually this reflects uncertainty and pessimism; collectively, indulging it causes the very collapse of aggregate demand and activity that agents fear.

**Why price adjustment fails:** Normally a rise in money demand lowers collective goods demand at going prices, suppliers compete, prices fall, and the falling price level revives spending — *unless* agents exhibit absolute liquidity preference. In a trap, falling prices do not revive spending because the desire to hoard money is unlimited.

**Why interest-rate adjustment fails:** Because money competes with interest-bearing stores of value, a rise in money demand normally cuts demand for such assets, issuers compete, the interest rate rises, and savers shift back into assets — eliminating the excess money demand. In a trap, because the desire to hoard is unlimited, this mechanism also ceases to work.
